parsed.study_design: Cross-sectional benefit-ranking survey with collaborative stakeholder workshops
parsed.population_and_sample: Fifty water-sector professionals from Kenya and Zambia, drawn from governance, finance/investment, engineering, mobile banking, human development, utilities and related fields; 58 participated in workshops and 50 completed surveys.
parsed.exposure: Mobile water-payment and smart-metering systems, including their associated governance, regulatory, financing and rural service-management models.
parsed.outcome: Professional rankings of eight potential benefits, including increased water-service coverage, improved payment processes and billing accuracy, flexible tariffs, new rural operation and maintenance models, system maintenance, leak/theft detection and water conservation.
parsed.rationale: Section 4 (pp. 438–439) reports an identifiable empirical survey: 58 professionals participated in structured workshops and 50 completed an anonymous ranking exercise concerning mobile-payment and smart-metering innovations. The measured benefit priorities include increased service coverage and new rural management models, and Section 5 (pp. 440–441) interprets country differences in relation to regulatory structures, sustainable finance, social equity and access for underserved rural populations. Although the sample is explicitly nonrepresentative and does not measure household-level effects, it provides empirical governance evidence relevant to mechanisms affecting water-service access.
